title: Emergent Ventures — prototype funding
summary: LaminarForge is building a modular heated drawer for tissue-on-chip plates. We seek funding to manufacture and test the first unit ourselves, establishing temperature performance, repeatability and cost before scaling.
proposal:
I’m Alex Lewis, and I’m developing LaminarForge to make experiments with tissue-on-chip plates easier to run at scale. My immediate focus is the equipment around a commercial plate: a temperature-controlled enclosure that can open for access and later fit into an automated system.

My background is in security platform engineering. At KnowBe4, my work includes production detection and response systems, security-event pipelines, cloud security and incident-response automation. I also build software and automation tools. With LaminarForge, I lead the hardware, CAD and firmware direction, documentation and validation planning. The project grew around making research tools more inspectable, reproducible and accessible. This prototype applies my systems-engineering experience to a physical instrument whose performance can be measured directly.

A mainstream view I agree with is that reliable experiments require reliable measurement. For this project, an aluminum heater reaching its setpoint is not enough. I need to measure the liquid inside the plate, how temperatures differ across it, and what happens when the enclosure opens. Those measurements will determine whether the design works.

My long-term objective is to support many independently accessible tissue plates without making each additional plate a complicated machine. The first step is deliberately small: one heated cassette, manufactured and evaluated before investing in a larger system.

The cassette has a fixed aluminum housing and a sliding heated drawer. A plate sits on the drawer, which opens for access from above. The housing and drawer each have their own heater, sensor and controller. A replaceable silicone gasket compresses at closure to reduce drafts. The prototype is manually operated. Later versions could add motorized access and mount to a rocking shelf if the selected tissue plate requires it.

The hypothesis is that this simple, repeatable module can provide stable plate temperatures while allowing frequent access, at a cost that makes replication practical. I am not claiming the individual components are new. The value I want to establish is in their integration: measured thermal performance, accessible plates and a straightforward path to making more identical units.

The design work has produced a fabrication package with STEP geometry, shop drawings, a parts list, wiring instructions and an assembly and test procedure. It was developed with AI-assisted research and CAD work. Automated geometry checks found no interference at the sampled drawer positions. These are design checks, not proof of physical performance. The cassette has not yet been manufactured or thermally validated.

I am requesting the amount detailed in the accompanying budget to manufacture and evaluate the prototype and fund one revision. The planning budget covers machining and finishing, heaters and controls, independent temperature-measurement equipment, test supplies, shipping and a reserve for rework. These are preliminary allowances, not supplier quotations. I would use supplier estimates to refine purchasing before spending. No matching personal cash contribution is assumed in this request.

I will run the validation internally, starting with water-filled plates. The first tests will check assembly fit, drawer motion and heater protection. Then I will measure temperatures in representative wells using calibrated probes and a separate logger. The proposed thermal targets are 36.5–37.5 degrees Celsius at every measured location, with no more than 0.5 degrees between the warmest and coolest locations at a given time. After a 30-second opening, the target is recovery into that band within ten minutes without exceeding 38 degrees at any measured location. These are proposed acceptance criteria, not results already achieved.

The work will also document power consumption, repeated opening and closing, visible wear and the actual cost of the build. If the initial unit misses its targets, I will use the measurements to guide one revision and repeat the affected tests. A documented failure is useful evidence; I will not substitute a heater reading or simulation for a successful liquid-temperature test.

The grant would produce an assembled prototype, raw measurement records, an account of the changes required, and a bill of materials grounded in actual purchases. The proposed schedule is twelve weeks from funding and access to a suitable workspace, subject to fabrication and instrument lead times: procurement and fabrication first, then assembly and baseline tests, followed by a revision and retest if necessary.

Successful water testing would establish one engineering prerequisite for tissue experiments. It would not establish cell viability, biological usefulness or compatibility with every commercial tissue plate. Those would be separate subsequent milestones.

The broader benefit I am pursuing is reducing the equipment burden of running many tissue experiments. This grant would turn an existing design into measurable evidence about whether the first module deserves further development.
budget_note: Planning allowances, not supplier quotes. No personal cash match assumed. Excludes salary, rent, living costs, robotics and biological experiments. Facility costs must be established before this is a complete project budget.
location: Prospective: Fitzsimons Innovation Community, Bioscience 1 / Suite 217, Aurora, Colorado. Identification is tentative; no space or permission secured. CUBiO is not the selected location.
notes: Organizational structure is undecided. Evaluate grants and investment on their merits. Application has not been submitted.
milestones:
1. Obtain fabrication and instrument estimates.
2. Assemble one manual heated cassette.
3. Check electrical protection and measure actual water temperatures.
4. Measure opening recovery and repeated drawer operation.
5. Make one revision if needed and record results and actual cost.
